reason: The contract explicitly requires a STABLE sort ('When two entries of a row hold the same key, the one with the LOWER original index must come first') and declares duplicate keys within a row to be expected. Kernel line 41 computes my_is_smaller = (keys < p_key) | ((keys == p_key) & (perm > p_perm)), i.e. among equal keys it treats the HIGHER original index as smaller — the inverse of stability. Probe t6 on the real kernel confirmed this at runtime: for keys=[2]*8 the kernel returns perm=[7,6,5,4,3,2,1,0] where stability requires [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7]; for [5,5,5,5,1,1,3,3] it returns perm=[5,4,7,6,3,2,1,0] vs the required [4,5,6,7,0,1,2,3] (each tied group reversed); on a 64x32 batch of quantized keys in [0,8), 64/64 rows disagree with torch stable argsort indices while the sorted values themselves are correct and non-decreasing, isolating the defect to tie order. Results were deterministic across repeats, so this is a systematic ordering rule, not a race. Additionally (t6 case B, W=7, non-power-of-two row): keys [1,1,1,0,0,5,5] produce kernel sorted output [0,1,0,1,1,5,5], which violates even the basic 'sorted_keys[n,:] is non-decreasing' requirement. Both failures lie squarely in the contract's declared input domain (arbitrary int64 keys with expected duplicates).
